item.title: [AFA 2025] Five Professors Spent Their Own Money on 85,000 Stock Trades to Find Out What "Free" Trading Really Costs
item.body:
> Researchers placed more than 85,000 identical, simultaneous stock orders at different brokerages and found the same trade can cost you noticeably different amounts depending on which app you use — a finding that earned the Dimensional Fund Advisors Distinguished Paper Prize, presented at the American Finance Association's 2025 annual meeting.

## What They Presented

"Zero commission" has been the headline promise of retail stock trading apps since 2019. But is a free trade actually free? Christopher Schwarz (UC Irvine), Brad Barber (UC Davis), Xing Huang (Washington University in St. Louis), Philippe Jorion (UC Irvine), and Terrance Odean (UC Berkeley) decided to test it the hard way: with real money, in real accounts.

From December 2021 to June 2022, the team opened six accounts at five different brokerages and submitted 85,417 market orders — buying and selling the same stocks, in the same quantities, at the same moments, across the different accounts. Because the orders were identical in every way except which broker handled them, any difference in the prices they got could only come from the brokers and the firms executing their trades. The experiment cost the researchers tens of thousands of dollars of their own trading losses.

The results were striking. The average cost of a "round trip" (buying and then selling a stock) ranged from about 0.07% at the best-performing account to about 0.46% at the worst — a gap of more than six times, even with zero commissions everywhere. On the very first day of the pilot, one account lost $150 while another account making the same trades gained $12.

Where does the gap come from? Most retail orders never reach a stock exchange. They are routed to off-exchange firms called wholesalers, which fill the orders and usually give customers a slightly better price than the official quote — so-called "price improvement." The study found that the same wholesalers systematically gave different amounts of price improvement to different brokers for essentially identical orders. Surprisingly, payment for order flow (PFOF) — the controversial money wholesalers pay brokers for sending them orders, and the usual suspect in this debate — did not explain the differences in execution prices across brokers.

The paper was published in the Journal of Finance, and the title's phrase "actual retail price" — familiar to anyone who has watched the game show The Price Is Right — hints at the point: the true price of a retail trade is not the one on the label.

## Why It Matters

Tens of millions of Americans now trade stocks through commission-free apps, and many pick a broker based on design, features, or marketing — assuming execution is the same everywhere. This study shows it is not. For an active trader, a few hundredths of a percent per trade compounds into real money over hundreds of trades a year.

The paper also reshaped a major policy debate. Regulators, including the SEC, had focused heavily on PFOF as the potential hidden cost of free trading. This evidence suggests the bigger issue is the lack of transparency around execution quality itself: brokers deliver measurably different prices, and nothing on your trade confirmation tells you so. As Schwarz put it, it is hard to think of another consumer financial product where costs differ this much without being disclosed. The authors propose more informative, standardized disclosures so investors can actually compare brokers on the thing that matters — the prices they get.

There is a professional lesson here too: the study's power comes from its design. Rather than analyzing messy historical data, the authors ran a clean field experiment — identical orders, same instant, different brokers — which is why a five-person academic team could produce evidence that moved an industry conversation.

## An Easy Way to Get It

Imagine identical twins walking into the same coffee shop at the same second and ordering the exact same latte — but each one orders through a different delivery app. Both apps advertise "no service fee." Yet one twin is quietly charged $4.93 and the other $5.15, because the coffee shop gives different behind-the-scenes discounts to different apps. Neither receipt shows a fee, so neither twin ever knows. That is essentially what this study documented in stock trading: same stock, same moment, same order — different price, depending on the app.

## In Three Lines

1. Researchers placed 85,000+ identical, simultaneous stock orders at five brokerages and found round-trip trading costs varied from roughly 0.07% to 0.46% across accounts, despite zero commissions.
2. The gap comes from wholesalers giving different price improvement to different brokers — and, contrary to expectations, payment for order flow did not explain the differences.
3. "Free" trading has a real, hidden price that varies by broker, and the authors call for clearer execution-quality disclosure so investors can compare.

## 📚 Today's Terms

- **Market order**: An instruction to buy or sell a stock immediately at the best available price, rather than at a price you specify.
- **Price improvement**: When your order is filled at a slightly better price than the official quoted price — for example, buying just under the posted asking price.
- **Payment for order flow (PFOF)**: Money that wholesalers pay brokerages in exchange for routing customer orders to them; a key reason brokers can charge zero commissions.
- **Wholesaler**: An off-exchange trading firm (such as a large market maker) that executes most retail stock orders instead of a public stock exchange.
- **Round-trip cost**: The total cost of buying a stock and then selling it, used here to measure how much value a trader loses to execution prices alone.
